title: Reaction rates, catalysts, energy and equilibrium
blurb: Use collision theory to predict what speeds up or slows a reaction, read an energy diagram and apply Le Chatelier's principle.
question: Enzymes speed up digestion, refrigerators slow food spoilage, and holding your breath lowers blood pH. What single set of ideas explains all three?

teach.body: Formally, collision theory states that particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy and in the correct orientation. In plain English: molecules have to bump into each other hard enough and the right way round. The reaction rate is how fast reactants become products. Anything that produces more effective collisions per second speeds the reaction up.

head: Change
Rate
Why
rows: More collisions, and more with enough energy
More particles per volume to collide
teach.caption: Nature of reactants matters too: ions in solution react fast; breaking strong covalent bonds is slow.

teach.body: Heating makes particles move faster, so they collide more often, but mainly a larger fraction of collisions now carries at least the activation energy. Many reactions roughly double in rate for each 10 °C rise; refrigeration slows food spoilage. A catalyst offers a pathway with lower activation energy. It is not used up, and it does not change the products, the overall energy change (ΔH) or the equilibrium position. Enzymes are biological catalysts; preservatives act as inhibitors.

teach.caption: The hill is the activation energy; the catalyst lowers it. Products end below reactants, so energy is released (ΔH negative). Both paths start and finish at the same levels.
Breaking bonds absorbs energy; forming bonds releases it. The balance between the two decides the sign of ΔH.

teach.body: In a reversible reaction, products can turn back into reactants. At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant, though usually not equal, while both reactions keep running. Le Chatelier's principle: if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, it shifts to counteract that stress.

teach.h: Le Chatelier's principle: stress and shift
head: Stress
Shift
teach.caption: Treat heat as a reactant in an endothermic reaction and as a product in an exothermic one.

teach.body: Imani, a nursing applicant, studies this equilibrium in blood: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. If a patient hypoventilates, CO₂ builds up (more reactant), so the system shifts right, producing more H⁺ and lowering blood pH (acidosis). Breathing fast blows off CO₂ (removing reactant), so it shifts left and pH rises.

teach.text: A catalyst LOWERS activation energy, is NOT used up and does NOT shift equilibrium. At equilibrium the reactions have not stopped and the amounts are not necessarily equal: the RATES are equal. Adding product shifts LEFT. Higher pressure favors the side with FEWER gas molecules.

items: Reactions need collisions with enough energy (activation energy) and the right orientation.
Higher temperature, concentration, pressure, surface area, stirring or a catalyst speed reactions; inhibitors slow them.
Catalysts (enzymes in the body) lower activation energy and are not consumed.
Exothermic: energy released, surroundings warm, ΔH negative. Endothermic: absorbed, cold, ΔH positive.
At equilibrium the rates are equal; Le Chatelier: the system shifts to counteract a stress.

summary: You can now predict how temperature, concentration, surface area, pressure, catalysts and inhibitors change a reaction's rate, and read an energy diagram for exothermic and endothermic reactions. You can also describe dynamic equilibrium and use Le Chatelier's principle to predict shifts, including in blood chemistry.

A.q: Why does crushing an antacid tablet make it react faster with stomach acid?
A.why: Smaller pieces expose more particles to the acid, so more collisions happen each second.

whyNot.1: A higher activation energy would slow the reaction, and crushing does not change it.
whyNot.2: Crushing does not change the mass of the tablet.
whyNot.3: Equilibrium position is about how far a reaction goes, not how fast; surface area changes the rate.

A.q: What does a catalyst do in a chemical reaction?
options: Is used up as the reaction runs
A.why: A catalyst gives the reaction an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed.

whyNot.0: Catalysts lower activation energy; raising it would slow the reaction.
whyNot.1: A catalyst is not consumed; it can be used again.
whyNot.3: A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not shift equilibrium.

A.q: An instant cold pack feels cold after it is squeezed and activated. The process inside the pack is:
A.why: The pack absorbs heat from its surroundings (your skin), so it feels cold: an endothermic process.

whyNot.0: Releasing heat would warm the pack, as a hand warmer does.
whyNot.1: Exothermic processes release heat; they do not absorb it.
whyNot.2: Endothermic processes absorb heat; they do not release it.

B.q: Which change would slow down a reaction between two solutions?
B.why: Diluting lowers concentration: fewer particles per volume means fewer collisions and a slower rate.

whyNot.2: Stirring brings reactants together and speeds the reaction.
whyNot.3: A catalyst lowers the activation energy and speeds the reaction.

B.q: Which statement describes a system at dynamic equilibrium?
options: Reactant and product amounts are equal
Forward and reverse rates are equal
B.why: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant.

whyNot.0: Both reactions keep running; that is what makes the equilibrium dynamic.
whyNot.1: Concentrations are constant, but they are usually not equal.
whyNot.2: If the forward reaction were faster, the system would not yet be at equilibrium.

B.q: For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g) at equilibrium, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium:
options: right, to the side with 2 gas moles
left, to the side with 4 gas moles
right, to the side with 4 gas moles
left, to the side with 2 gas moles
B.why: The left side has 1 + 3 = 4 moles of gas; the right has 2. Higher pressure favors fewer gas moles, so it shifts right.

whyNot.1: Higher pressure favors the side with FEWER gas moles; the left side's 4 is the larger total.
whyNot.2: The right side has 2 gas moles (2 NH₃), not 4.
whyNot.3: The left side has 1 + 3 = 4 gas moles, not 2.

C.q: The reaction A + B ⇌ C + heat is at equilibrium. What happens if the temperature is lowered?
options: It shifts left, making more A and B
It has no effect on the equilibrium
It shifts right, making more C
It shifts right, absorbing more heat
C.why: Heat is a product (exothermic forward reaction). Removing heat is like removing a product, so the system shifts right and makes more C.

whyNot.0: Shifting left would absorb heat; that is the response to RAISING the temperature.
whyNot.1: Temperature changes do shift equilibrium; only a catalyst leaves it unchanged.
whyNot.3: The forward (right) direction releases heat here; it does not absorb it.

C.q: Raising the temperature speeds up most reactions mainly because:
options: a bigger share of collisions is energetic
the activation energy of the reaction drops
the particles become larger and collide more
the products become more stable than before
C.why: Faster-moving particles collide more often, but the main effect is that more collisions have at least the activation energy.

whyNot.1: Temperature does not change the activation energy; a catalyst does.
whyNot.2: Particles move faster when heated; they do not grow larger.
whyNot.3: Product stability (ΔH) is unchanged by temperature; the rate change comes from collision energy.

C.q: A patient hypoventilates and CO₂ builds up. Using CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, what should you predict?
C.why: Adding a reactant (CO₂) shifts the equilibrium right, producing more H⁺. More H⁺ means lower pH (acidosis).

whyNot.0: Shifting left happens when CO₂ is removed, as in fast breathing.
whyNot.2: Shifting right makes more H⁺, which lowers pH rather than raising it.
whyNot.3: Adding a reactant is a stress, so the system does shift.

reteach.title: A mall with two escalators
reteach.question: Picture a two-floor mall with an up escalator and a down escalator running all day. How does it explain equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle?

blocks.body: Shoppers ride up (forward reaction) and down (reverse reaction) all day. Once as many people ride up per minute as ride down, the number on each floor stays steady, even though the floors need not hold equal crowds and the escalators never stop. That is dynamic equilibrium. Send a busload of shoppers to the ground floor (add reactant) and more people head upstairs until it balances again: Le Chatelier.

blocks.text: A catalyst is like speeding up BOTH escalators equally: the mall reaches its balance sooner, but the final crowd on each floor is the same. It does not shift equilibrium.

explain.body: Rate rises with temperature, concentration, gas pressure, surface area, stirring and catalysts, because each gives more effective collisions. Inhibitors and cooling slow reactions.

test.q: Food keeps longer in a refrigerator mainly because:
test.why: At lower temperature fewer collisions carry the activation energy, so spoilage reactions slow down.

whyNot.0: Cold air holds the same proportion of oxygen; temperature is what changes.
whyNot.1: Cooling does not add a catalyst; catalysts speed reactions up.
whyNot.2: Activation energy is a property of the pathway; temperature changes how many collisions reach it.

explain.body: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, speeds the reaction and is not consumed. It does not change the products, ΔH or the equilibrium position. Enzymes are the body's catalysts.

test.q: Which statement about enzymes is correct?
options: They are used up in each reaction
They raise the energy of reactants
test.why: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower the activation energy and are not consumed.

whyNot.0: Catalysts, including enzymes, are not consumed and can be reused.
whyNot.2: Catalysts do not change what is produced, only how fast.
whyNot.3: Enzymes lower the energy barrier; they do not add energy to the reactants.

explain.body: Exothermic reactions release energy (surroundings warm, ΔH negative); endothermic reactions absorb it (surroundings cool, ΔH positive). Activation energy is the hill every reaction must climb.

test.q: Which is true of an exothermic reaction?
test.why: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, so the products end with less energy than the reactants.

whyNot.0: Surroundings cool in an endothermic reaction; exothermic ones warm them.
whyNot.1: A positive ΔH means energy was absorbed (endothermic).
whyNot.3: In an exothermic reaction the products store less energy than the reactants.

explain.body: At equilibrium, forward rate = reverse rate. A stress shifts the system to counteract it: add reactant, shift right; add product, shift left; raise pressure, toward fewer gas moles.

test.q: A reaction is at equilibrium. Adding more of the product will:
test.why: The system counteracts the extra product by running the reverse reaction faster, shifting left toward reactants.

whyNot.1: Shifting right would make even more product; that follows adding reactant.
whyNot.2: Changing a concentration is a stress, so the position shifts.
whyNot.3: Extra product speeds the reverse reaction up rather than stopping it.
